_doc: docs/component-catalog.md — edges of the component↔problem graph. Keyed by component id, then by design-problem unit id. Each value says WHAT THE COMPONENT IS DOING in that problem, phrased as a predicate about the job so the same string reads correctly rendered at either endpoint. Gate 5 in validate-system-design.js requires an entry for every problem tagged with a component's mechanism.

caching.p01: Hot short-code → long-URL lookups. The mapping is immutable once created, so there is no invalidation story to get wrong — only capacity and TTL.
caching.p02: The per-user timeline of post IDs in Redis, hydrated to full post bodies on read. The cache IS the precomputed feed, not an optimisation over it.
caching.p08: The counter state itself. Limiter state is small, extremely hot, and worthless once stale — which is exactly the shape an in-memory store is for.
caching.p11: Top-N slices per leaderboard window, so the overwhelmingly common 'show me the top 100' read never touches the underlying ranking structure.
caching.p12: The whole problem. Ring placement, replication and eviction all exist to make one cache survive nodes joining and leaving without losing its value.
caching.p14: Precomputed top-K completions per prefix, held in memory because the keystroke budget is tens of milliseconds and a rebuild is a batch job.
caching.p16: Event and seat-map reads, which vastly outnumber bookings. Availability counts are cached loosely on purpose; the actual hold stays transactional.
caching.p22: Prompt-prefix and KV-cache reuse across requests, so a shared system prompt is not recomputed per call — the dominant saving in LLM serving.
caching.p24: Popular geo cells, whose query volume is wildly skewed toward a few dense urban areas. A short TTL absorbs most reads before the index sees them.
caching.p30: The online store is a cache by another name: precomputed features in a low-latency store, because inference cannot wait for a batch job to finish.
caching.p32: Session and token-validation state, so every authenticated request is not a database read. Revocation is what makes the TTL choice genuinely hard.
caching.p34: Adjudications are cached rather than raw matches, so a name a human already cleared against the current list version does not re-enter the review queue on every payment.

sharding.p01: Splits the mapping table by short-code hash once one primary cannot hold the row count. Access is pure key lookup, which shards about as cleanly as anything does.
sharding.p11: Partitions scores by leaderboard and time window; one global sorted set would concentrate every write in the system on a single node.
sharding.p14: The trie is partitioned by prefix — the textbook uneven partition, since 'a' and 'th' carry orders of magnitude more traffic than 'zq'.
sharding.p21: The core mechanic. The keyspace is divided across nodes by ring position, and every other feature in the design is built on top of that division.
sharding.p24: Geo cells are the partition key, so nearby entities land on the same node. Locality is the point; population skew is the price you agree to pay.
sharding.p25: The index is split document-wise so each shard holds a slice of the corpus; a query scatters to every shard and gathers the top-K.
sharding.p26: Telemetry is partitioned by series or tenant, because ingest volume is the defining constraint and no single node absorbs a firehose.

idempotency.p07: Deduplicates sends, so an at-least-once redelivery does not mean the user's phone buzzes twice for one event.
idempotency.p15: The client-supplied key on every transfer, recorded in the same transaction as the ledger entry — the difference between a retry and a double charge.
idempotency.p16: Booking requests carry a key, so a double-tap or a lost response does not leave one user holding two seats for the same show.
idempotency.p17: Orders must survive retry without dispensing twice; the key is recorded with the fulfilment record, not before it.
idempotency.p20: A job execution is keyed, so at-least-once dispatch does not run the same scheduled task twice on two different workers.
idempotency.p29: The delivery id sent with every request, so receivers can recognise a redelivery. Its absence is what makes at-least-once dangerous for them.
idempotency.p32: Token issuance and refresh are made repeat-safe, so a retried login does not mint a second live session the user cannot see or revoke.
idempotency.p33: A redelivered alert file must not re-investigate what was already decided, so the key is the source alert id and revision rather than anything the pipeline generates.
idempotency.p36: A vendor timeout is ambiguous about whether the work happened, so the retry has to record one result and incur one charge no matter how many attempts it took.

replication.p12: Each entry is held on N successive ring nodes, so losing one node degrades the hit rate instead of losing a whole slice of the keyspace.
replication.p15: Synchronous replication of the ledger, because losing an acknowledged financial write is not a degraded mode — it is an unrecoverable defect.
replication.p19: Each partition has a leader and followers; the in-sync replica set is what lets an acknowledged publish survive a broker dying.
replication.p21: N replicas per key range with tunable W and R — where this problem's entire consistency-versus-availability conversation actually lives.
replication.p25: Index shards are replicated for read throughput and node loss. Query volume, not durability, is what drives the replica count here.
replication.p32: Session state is replicated across regions, so a login in one region is honoured in another without a cross-region read on every request.

fanout.p02: The central tradeoff: push each post into every follower's timeline on write, or assemble on read — with the hybrid as the production answer.
fanout.p03: New photos are pushed into follower feeds, carrying the same celebrity write-amplification problem and the same hybrid escape hatch.
fanout.p06: One message delivered to every member of a group conversation — a fan-out over live connections rather than over stored timelines.
fanout.p07: One triggering event expanded into per-user, per-channel deliveries, with email, push and SMS each a separate send from a single source event.
fanout.p27: One encoded stream distributed to the entire audience at once, where the fan-out degree is the viewer count and the CDN is what makes it affordable.

ranking.p02: Orders the assembled timeline by recency, affinity and engagement rather than pure chronology — the second half of the feed problem after fan-out.
ranking.p23: Reranks vector-retrieved candidates before they reach the model, because approximate-nearest-neighbour recall is not the same thing as relevance.
ranking.p25: Scores matching documents so the top-K is worth reading. Retrieval finds candidates; ranking is what makes the result page useful.
ranking.p28: Drives the entire product. The feed is not a follow graph but a ranked stream, so the ranker IS the short-form video experience.
ranking.p31: Prioritises the review queue so the most likely violations and the highest-reach content reach a human moderator first.
ranking.p34: Scoring the surviving candidates is where date of birth, nationality and identifiers separate a genuine hit from a common surname, and it produces three bands rather than a boolean.

work-queue.p05: The URL frontier — the crawler's queue of what to fetch next, with politeness and priority encoded in how items are dequeued.
work-queue.p07: Decouples the triggering event from delivery, so a slow SMS provider cannot block push notifications or the request that caused them.
work-queue.p20: The dispatch path: due jobs are enqueued and worker pools pull from it, which is what separates deciding-what-is-due from running-it.
work-queue.p22: Inference requests wait for scarce GPU capacity rather than being rejected outright, with queue depth feeding the admission decision.
work-queue.p31: Content awaiting automated scoring and human review moves through queues, decoupling upload throughput from review capacity.
work-queue.p33: Alerts arrive as an overnight batch and each investigation runs for minutes, so the queue is what decouples a 4K-alert dump from a fixed pool of concurrent investigations.
work-queue.p35: The workers are people, so the queue hands out leases rather than assignments and reclaims anything a reviewer abandons without needing the client to cooperate.
work-queue.p36: Verification hops have wildly different latencies, from a 2-second API call to a manual check taking days, so the work is queued per hop rather than held open per application.

backpressure.p05: Politeness limits and frontier depth bound how fast the crawler pulls, so it neither melts a target site nor outruns its own parsers.
backpressure.p19: Producers are slowed when partitions cannot absorb writes, because the alternative is unbounded broker storage followed by a hard failure.
backpressure.p22: Queue depth signals the admission controller to reject or shed, rather than accumulating requests that will time out before a GPU frees up.
backpressure.p26: Ingest pushes back on agents when the pipeline saturates — dropping telemetry is preferable to the observability platform collapsing under it.
backpressure.p29: A slow or dead receiver must not consume unbounded delivery capacity; per-endpoint concurrency limits stop one customer starving the rest.
backpressure.p33: Per-tenant concurrency caps keep one bank's overnight backfill from consuming every worker slot, because the shared ceiling is model and vendor spend rather than CPU.

rate-limiting.p05: Per-domain politeness. The crawler caps its own request rate per host — a limiter pointed at itself rather than at incoming callers.
rate-limiting.p08: The problem itself. Every decision here is about where the counter lives and how exact it needs to be across a fleet of gateways.
rate-limiting.p29: Delivery attempts per receiver endpoint are capped, so retries toward a struggling customer do not turn into an attack on them.
rate-limiting.p31: Caps per-uploader submission rate — the cheapest defence against bulk spam, applied before any model spends compute on the content.
rate-limiting.p32: Login attempts per account and per IP, the primary defence against credential stuffing and brute force.
rate-limiting.p34: Escalations are throttled into the review queue rather than at the matcher, because matching is cheap and the humans are the bottleneck that a list delta would otherwise flood.
rate-limiting.p35: Admission into the queue is metered per lane, so a 500K-item batch dump drains gradually instead of displacing the live stream that has deadlines attached.

hot-keys.p02: The celebrity account: one write with tens of millions of followers, which is precisely the case that breaks naive fan-out-on-write.
hot-keys.p11: One popular leaderboard absorbs most of the reads and writes, so its sorted set has to be split or replicated away from the others.
hot-keys.p18: A viral campaign concentrates click events on a single aggregation key, saturating whichever partition happens to own it.
hot-keys.p24: Dense urban cells hold vastly more entities and receive vastly more queries than the rest of the grid, by orders of magnitude.

cdn.p03: Serves the image bytes themselves, so origin egress does not scale with viewer count and users fetch from a nearby PoP.
cdn.p04: Distributes video segments — the economics of the whole design, since origin bandwidth for video is the cost that dominates everything else.
cdn.p27: Delivers HLS/DASH segments to viewers, which is what makes a million-concurrent-viewer broadcast affordable at all.
cdn.p28: Prefetches and serves the next videos in the feed, because perceived instant playback is the product's core interaction.

websockets.p06: Holds the client connection so inbound messages are pushed instantly, with presence and delivery receipts riding the same channel.
websockets.p09: Carries continuous driver location updates and ride-match offers — both server-initiated and both latency-critical.
websockets.p10: Streams each operation to every other collaborator, which is the only way the shared-cursor experience can feel live.
websockets.p27: Powers chat and reactions alongside the video, providing the interactive layer a segment-based CDN path structurally cannot.

aggregation.p11: Scores are maintained as running totals rather than recomputed, so a read is a range query on a sorted set instead of a scan.
aggregation.p18: The output of the system: click counts per ad per window, maintained incrementally because the raw stream is far too large to scan on demand.
aggregation.p26: Metrics are pre-rolled into time buckets at ingest, so a dashboard query reads summaries instead of scanning raw telemetry.
aggregation.p30: Windowed feature values — counts and averages over recent activity — computed once and served to every model that needs them.

stream-processing.p18: Windowed counting over the click firehose, where watermarks and late-event policy decide what a given 'minute' actually contains.
stream-processing.p26: Telemetry is enriched, sampled and aggregated in flight, because storing everything raw and querying later meets neither the cost nor latency bar.
stream-processing.p30: Real-time features are derived from event streams as they arrive — what makes an online feature fresher than a nightly batch job.
stream-processing.p31: Uploads flow through a scoring pipeline continuously, so moderation decisions land within seconds of publish rather than on a schedule.

blob-storage.p03: Holds the original photos and their derived sizes; the database stores only metadata and the object key that points at them.
blob-storage.p04: Stores raw uploads and every transcoded rendition, which is why storage cost multiplies by the size of the bitrate ladder.
blob-storage.p13: The backing store for content-addressed chunks, with the file manifest in a database pointing at each one.
blob-storage.p36: The uploaded document is evidence with the same retention obligation as the decision, so the original is content-addressed and never replaced by anything derived from it.

transcoding.p04: Converts each upload into the full bitrate ladder, so players can adapt to changing network conditions mid-playback.
transcoding.p27: Must run in near-real-time against live ingest, which is exactly what makes it harder here than in the on-demand case.
transcoding.p28: Produces the short vertical renditions and thumbnails, at a volume driven by upload rate rather than by watch time.

ordering.p06: Messages within one conversation must appear in the same order for every participant, which pins a conversation to a single partition.
ordering.p10: Operations on a document must apply in an agreed sequence — the thing the OT or CRDT machinery exists to establish.
ordering.p19: Per-partition ordering is the guarantee the broker sells; global ordering is deliberately not offered because it would serialise everything.
ordering.p35: Arrival order carries no information about importance, so the queue orders by risk and deadline with an aging term that bounds how long the tail can wait.

at-least-once.p07: A notification may arrive twice but must never be silently dropped, which is what sets the deduplication requirement downstream.
at-least-once.p20: A scheduled job may fire twice if a worker dies mid-run, so job bodies have to tolerate re-execution by construction.
at-least-once.p29: The contract offered to receivers — retried until acknowledged — which is why every delivery carries an id they can dedupe on.
at-least-once.p33: Alert delivery is retried by the bank and by the transport, so the pipeline assumes duplicates by default and makes the investigation step safe to repeat rather than trying to deduplicate at the edge.

consistent-hashing.p08: Routes each client key to the node holding its counter, so limiter state is not remapped every time a gateway is added or removed.
consistent-hashing.p12: Places keys on the ring so adding a node moves ~1/N of them, instead of invalidating the whole cache and stampeding the origin.
consistent-hashing.p21: Assigns key ranges to nodes and defines the replica set as the next N nodes clockwise from the key's ring position.

reservation.p09: A driver is held for a rider while the offer is outstanding, so two riders cannot be matched to the same car.
reservation.p16: Seats are held for the duration of checkout with an expiry — the mechanism that prevents overselling without locking for the whole session.
reservation.p17: Stock is held while the order and its authorisation clear, since dispensing against inventory that is already gone is not recoverable.
reservation.p35: A claimed item is held under an expiring lease, which gives at-most-one-active-reviewer without a lock service and returns the item automatically when someone closes their laptop.

conflict-resolution.p10: Concurrent edits to the same region are merged rather than rejected — the decision that makes collaborative editing feel live instead of contested.
conflict-resolution.p13: Two devices editing the same file offline produce divergent versions, and the design must choose between merging and conflicted copies.
conflict-resolution.p21: Concurrent writes accepted by different replicas are reconciled with version vectors, since a quorum permits them by construction.
conflict-resolution.p36: The document, the registry and the applicant will state different addresses, so precedence is declared in advance and the winning source is recorded rather than silently overwriting.

search-index.p14: The prefix-to-completions structure that turns each keystroke into a lookup rather than a scan over the query log.
search-index.p23: Keyword retrieval running alongside vector search, because hybrid retrieval consistently beats either one alone on real queries.
search-index.p25: The inverted index is the system: term → posting list is what makes query time independent of corpus size.
search-index.p34: Alias, transliteration and spelling expansion turn 40K sanctioned entities into millions of searchable strings, so candidate generation runs over an n-gram index rather than the entity list.

dedup.p05: URL and content deduplication, so the crawler neither re-fetches a page nor stores identical content under two different addresses.
dedup.p13: Content-addressed chunks mean an identical block uploaded by any user is stored once — where the storage savings in this design come from.

geo-index.p09: Indexes driver locations by cell, so 'nearby available drivers' is a range scan rather than a distance calculation across the fleet.
geo-index.p24: The core structure: businesses indexed by geohash or S2 cell, with neighbouring cells scanned to catch results just over a boundary.

chunking.p13: Files are split so only changed blocks transfer on edit, which is what makes syncing a large file after a small change cheap.
chunking.p23: Documents are split into passages small enough to embed meaningfully and to fit a context window, with overlap so meaning survives the cut.

exactly-once.p15: A transfer must debit and credit exactly once; a duplicate here is money moved twice, so the ledger write and the dedup record commit together.
exactly-once.p18: Click counts must not double under retry, which is why the aggregation sink and the offset commit are made atomic with each other.

saga.p15: A transfer spanning accounts or external processors proceeds as compensable steps, because no distributed transaction spans them.
saga.p17: Order → payment → pharmacy fulfilment crosses systems, and each step needs a compensation because some of them cannot be rolled back at all.

leader-election.p19: Each partition has exactly one leader accepting writes, and electing a new one on failure is what lets the broker survive node loss.
leader-election.p20: Exactly one scheduler instance may decide which jobs are due, or every due job fires once per running instance.

feature-serving.p28: User and video features are fetched at request time to score the candidate set inside the feed's latency budget.
feature-serving.p30: The problem itself — the online/offline split and point-in-time correctness are the entire design.

id-generation.p01: Produces the short code itself. Counter-encoding versus random-with-collision-check versus hashing is the heart of this problem.

resource-scheduling.p22: GPU allocation across requests, where continuous batching and priority classes decide whether very expensive hardware sits idle.

vector-search.p23: Retrieves passages by embedding similarity, which is what lets a question phrased differently from the source document still find it.

audit-trail.p15: A double-entry ledger is the audit trail: the balance is derived from immutable entries rather than stored, so any figure can be re-proved from the entries that produced it.
audit-trail.p18: Raw events are kept in object storage and a nightly batch recompute is the authority, so the fast streaming number is always reconcilable against a durable record of what actually arrived.
audit-trail.p33: An examiner can ask years later why one alert was cleared, so the trace pins prompt, model snapshot, policy version and evidence hashes — everything whose change would change the answer.
audit-trail.p35: A reviewer's decision is written as an immutable event with its reason and the lease that authorised it, and a correction references the original rather than overwriting it.
audit-trail.p36: Sources disagree routinely, so the record keeps what each one said and which precedence rule decided between them, rather than silently keeping the winner.

cost-metering.p22: GPU seconds are the scarce resource and the KV cache sets how many sequences fit, so admission is a spend decision per request rather than a queueing one.
cost-metering.p33: An agent choosing its own tools is spending money autonomously, so each case carries a hard budget and cost becomes an input to tool selection rather than a report afterwards.
cost-metering.p36: A full ownership walk can fire dozens of paid lookups, so checks are ordered by cost and information gain and results are cached per entity across applications.

agent-decision-record.p33: Every auto-closed alert carries the reason code it closed under, the agent's confidence, the threshold in force that day, and whether a reviewer later disagreed.
agent-decision-record.p35: The reviewer's verdict is stored beside the agent's recommendation rather than replacing it, so the disagreement rate is a number instead of an impression.
agent-decision-record.p36: A verification records which source it believed and how sure it was, so an approval on thin evidence is visible rather than indistinguishable from a confident one.

progressive-rollout.p31: New models shadow live traffic and their decisions are compared before enforcing, and the auto-remove and auto-approve bands widen only as far as the score distribution has been shown to hold.
progressive-rollout.p33: Autonomy is earned per alert type: the agent runs alongside analysts first, then recommends, and only auto-closes the narrowest band where its disposition has already matched theirs.

tenant-isolation.p20: One tenant flooding the scheduler with jobs must not starve another's, so admission and worker capacity are partitioned rather than shared first-come-first-served.
tenant-isolation.p26: A single tenant's cardinality explosion must not evict another tenant's series, so limits are enforced per tenant at the gateway rather than as one global ceiling.
